subject: Welding and Fabrication
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a practical test of 3 hours 10 minutes with one compulsory question for 100 marks; the materials list is released at least two weeks before. Candidates mark out, cut, form, join (weld, rivet, solder or bolt) and finish a job from a drawing, and are marked on accuracy, weld/joint quality, finish and safe working (an alternative paper may be used where materials cannot be acquired).

practicals.title: Use of protective wear and workshop safety in welding
practicals.topic: Safety Precautions in Welding and Fabrication Workshop
practicals.aim: To identify and correctly wear the protective equipment for welding and fabrication and to apply workshop safety rules.
apparatus: Welding helmet with correct shade filter (arc) and gas welding goggles
safety: Never look at an arc with the naked eye — arc eye can result within seconds.
Keep flammable materials at least 10 m from welding or shield them.
Ensure good ventilation to remove fumes.
procedure: Identify each item of PPE and state the hazard it protects against.
Put on PPE in order: overalls (cotton, no turn-ups), boots, apron, gauntlets, helmet.
Check the helmet filter shade for the welding current.
Inspect the work area: screens, ventilation, fire extinguisher, no oil on floor.
Locate the main isolator and the first aid box.
Demonstrate the action on discovering a fire or burn.
practicals.expectedObservations: All PPE is worn correctly and the work area meets the checklist.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Filter shade guide (typical): MMA welding at 60–150 A uses shade 10–11; 150–250 A uses shade 12; gas welding uses shade 4–6 goggles. A student welding at 100 A therefore uses at least shade 10.
precautions: Replace cracked filter lenses immediately.
Keep sleeves rolled down and collars buttoned.
sourcesOfError: Using too light a filter for the current.
commonMistakes: Wearing synthetic clothing that melts.
Using gas goggles for arc welding.
examTips: List hazards with matching protection: UV/IR radiation, spatter, fumes, electric shock, fire, noise.
Mention environmental pollution control: fume extraction and proper disposal of slag and scraps.

checkQuestions.q: Arc eye is caused by
checkQuestions.explanation: UV burns the cornea.

checkQuestions.q: The suitable fire extinguisher for an electrical fire is
checkQuestions.explanation: They do not conduct electricity.

checkQuestions.q: Gas welding goggles are
checkQuestions.explanation: Arc welding needs much darker shades.

practicals.title: Identifying metals by appearance and spark test
practicals.aim: To identify common workshop metals by appearance, weight, magnet test and the grinder spark test.
materials: Samples: mild steel, high-carbon (tool) steel, cast iron, stainless steel, aluminium, copper, brass, zinc
safety: Wear goggles and keep the tool rest close to the wheel during spark tests.
Do not grind non-ferrous metals on the wheel (they clog it).
procedure: Observe colour and surface of each sample.
Test each with a magnet.
File a corner and note hardness and colour of the filed surface.
Spark-test ferrous samples with light pressure in a dim area.
Compare relative weights of equal-sized samples.
Record and identify each metal.
practicals.expectedObservations: Mild steel gives long straw-coloured streaks with few bursts; high-carbon steel gives many bright bushy bursts; cast iron gives short dull red streaks. Aluminium, copper and brass are non-magnetic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Relative weight check: equal 50 × 50 × 10 mm blocks (25 cm³) weigh about 196 g (steel, 7.85 g/cm³), 68 g (aluminium, 2.70 g/cm³) and 224 g (copper, 8.96 g/cm³).
precautions: Use light pressure for spark tests.
Compare against known samples.
commonMistakes: Spark-testing aluminium on the grinder.
Assuming stainless steel is always magnetic.
examTips: Classify metals as ferrous/non-ferrous with examples and uses.
Describe the spark pattern for mild steel, high-carbon steel and cast iron.

checkQuestions.q: Which metal is non-ferrous?
checkQuestions.explanation: Non-ferrous metals contain no iron.

checkQuestions.q: Many bright, bursting sparks indicate
checkQuestions.explanation: Carbon bursts produce the forks.

checkQuestions.q: Brass is an alloy of
checkQuestions.explanation: Bronze is copper and tin.

practicals.title: Annealing, hardening and tempering steel
practicals.aim: To harden and temper a high-carbon steel cold chisel and to anneal and normalise samples, observing the changes in properties.
materials: High-carbon steel bar (e.g. old file or chisel blank)
safety: Wear apron, gloves and goggles; quenching oil may flash.
Treat all metal as hot; mark hot pieces.
procedure: Anneal: heat a steel sample to cherry red and cool slowly in ashes or sand; test with a file and by bending.
Normalise: heat to the same temperature and cool in still air.
Harden: heat the chisel tip to cherry red (about 780–820 °C) and quench vertically in water.
Test with a file: it should skate.
Clean one side bright with emery cloth.
Temper: reheat the shank slowly and watch the oxide colours run to the tip; quench when the tip is purple to dark blue.
Compare the properties of each sample.
practicals.expectedObservations: Annealed steel is soft and bends easily; hardened steel is file-hard but brittle; tempered steel is tough. Tempering colours appear in sequence: pale straw, dark straw, brown, purple, blue.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Approximate tempering colours: pale straw ≈ 230 °C (lathe tools), dark straw ≈ 245 °C (drills), brown ≈ 255 °C, purple ≈ 270 °C (cold chisels), dark blue ≈ 300 °C (springs). A cold chisel is quenched at purple, about 270 °C.
precautions: Quench with a vertical up-and-down motion to avoid distortion.
Clean the surface bright before tempering so colours are visible.
sourcesOfError: Judging temperature by colour in bright light.
commonMistakes: Skipping tempering, leaving a brittle tool.
Overheating and burning the steel.
examTips: Define each process with heating, soaking and cooling method and resulting property.
Note: copper is annealed by heating and quenching.

checkQuestions.q: Annealing makes steel
checkQuestions.explanation: Slow cooling produces a soft structure.

checkQuestions.q: Tempering is done after hardening to
checkQuestions.explanation: It trades some hardness for toughness.

checkQuestions.q: A cold chisel is tempered to about
checkQuestions.explanation: It needs toughness for impact.

practicals.title: Setting up oxy-acetylene equipment and adjusting flames
practicals.topic: Equipment Set-up for Gas and Arc Welding and Fabrication
practicals.aim: To assemble oxy-acetylene equipment safely, light the blowpipe and produce carburising, neutral and oxidising flames.
apparatus: Oxygen (black) and acetylene (maroon) cylinders on a trolley
safety: Keep cylinders upright and chained; acetylene must never lie on its side.
Never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings — risk of explosion.
Fit flashback arrestors; know how to shut down in a backfire.
procedure: Crack each cylinder valve briefly to blow out dust (away from people and flames).
Fit regulators (acetylene left-hand thread, oxygen right-hand thread), arrestors, hoses and blowpipe.
Open cylinder valves slowly; set working pressures for the nozzle size.
Test all joints with leak-test solution.
Purge each hose; open acetylene, light with the spark lighter; then add oxygen.
Adjust to carburising, then neutral (inner cone clear, feather just gone), then oxidising.
Shut down: acetylene off first, then oxygen; close cylinders, bleed lines and release regulator screws.
practicals.expectedObservations: Carburising flame has a feather around the inner cone; neutral flame has a clear rounded inner cone; oxidising flame has a short pointed cone and a hissing sound.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Acetylene should not be withdrawn faster than about one-fifth of the cylinder content per hour. From a 7 m³ cylinder the maximum withdrawal is 7/5 = 1.4 m³/h; larger nozzles need cylinders coupled in a manifold.
precautions: Light acetylene first and shut it off first.
Never use acetylene above 1.0 bar (15 psi).
sourcesOfError: Incorrect pressure for the nozzle giving backfires.
commonMistakes: Using matches or cigarette lighters.
Testing for leaks with a flame.
examTips: Give the colour codes of cylinders and hoses and the thread directions.
Describe the three flames and their uses (neutral for steel, oxidising for brass, carburising for hard-facing).

checkQuestions.q: When shutting down, the first valve closed is the
checkQuestions.explanation: Fuel off first to avoid soot and flashback.

checkQuestions.q: The flame used for welding mild steel is
checkQuestions.explanation: It neither adds carbon nor oxidises the weld.

checkQuestions.q: Oxygen fittings must never be lubricated with oil because
options: oil can ignite violently in pure oxygen
checkQuestions.explanation: Oxygen and oil react explosively.

practicals.title: Preparing acetylene gas from calcium carbide
practicals.topic: Preparation of Acetylene Gas from Carbide
practicals.aim: To demonstrate on a small scale the production of acetylene from calcium carbide and water and to calculate the theoretical yield.
apparatus: Gas jar or test tubes over water (trough)
Splint (for testing small samples only, under supervision)
materials: A few lumps of calcium carbide
safety: Demonstration only, done by the teacher in the open air or a fume cupboard.
Acetylene is highly flammable and forms explosive mixtures with air; no flames near the apparatus.
Store carbide in a sealed dry tin; it reacts with moisture.
procedure: Place a few small lumps of carbide in the dry flask.
Add water drop by drop from the funnel.
Collect the gas over water.
Observe the gas (colourless, garlic-like smell from impurities).
Test a small test tube of gas at arm's length: it burns with a smoky yellow flame.
Dispose of the lime residue safely.
practicals.expectedObservations: Effervescence occurs as water touches the carbide; a white sludge of calcium hydroxide remains. The gas burns with a very smoky flame in air.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂. Molar mass CaC₂ = 64.1 g/mol. 1 kg of pure carbide = 1 000/64.1 = 15.6 mol, giving 15.6 mol C₂H₂ = 15.6 × 22.4 ≈ 349 L at s.t.p. (commercial carbide gives less because it is not pure).
precautions: Add water slowly to control the rate.
Keep the generator cool.
commonMistakes: Adding a large amount of water at once.
Storing carbide in damp containers.
examTips: Write the balanced equation.
Explain why cylinder acetylene is dissolved in acetone in a porous mass.

checkQuestions.q: Calcium carbide reacts with water to give
checkQuestions.explanation: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂.

checkQuestions.q: Acetylene in cylinders is dissolved in
checkQuestions.explanation: Acetone in a porous filler stabilises it.

checkQuestions.q: One mole of CaC₂ produces how many moles of C₂H₂?
checkQuestions.explanation: The equation ratio is 1:1.

practicals.title: Using measuring and marking-out tools
practicals.topic: Measuring Instruments, Marking Out and Cutting Tools
practicals.aim: To use the steel rule, vernier caliper, micrometer, scriber, dividers, centre punch and try square to mark out and check a job.
safety: Keep scriber points covered when not in use.
procedure: Coat the plate with marking blue.
Establish a datum edge and square lines from it.
Scribe lines using the rule and square.
Mark hole centres and circles with dividers; centre-punch lightly.
Measure the plate thickness with the micrometer and width with the vernier.
Record readings and compare with the drawing.
practicals.expectedObservations: Clean, fine lines visible against the blue; measurements agree with the drawing to within ±0.1 mm.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Vernier reading: main scale 23 mm, vernier line 14 coincides at 0.02 mm per division → 23 + 14 × 0.02 = 23.28 mm. Micrometer: sleeve 5.5 mm + thimble 28 × 0.01 = 5.78 mm.
precautions: Measure from a datum to avoid accumulated errors.
Do not over-tighten measuring instruments.
commonMistakes: Ignoring zero error.
Heavy centre punching that distorts thin sheet.
examTips: Show the reading working clearly.
Name each tool and its use.

checkQuestions.q: Main scale 12 mm, vernier coincidence 7 (0.02 mm). Reading =
Marking blue is used to
checkQuestions.explanation: It contrasts with bright scribed lines.

checkQuestions.q: Dividers are used for
options: scribing circles and stepping off distances
checkQuestions.explanation: They transfer and step distances.

practicals.title: Striking an arc and running straight beads
practicals.aim: To strike and maintain an arc with a manual metal arc (MMA) welder and deposit straight, uniform beads on a mild steel plate.
safety: Wear full PPE; erect screens to protect others.
Keep cables dry and undamaged; do not change electrodes with bare hands.
Chip slag with goggles on, away from your face.
procedure: Clean the plate and attach the earth clamp securely.
Set the current for the electrode size.
Strike the arc by the scratching or tapping method.
Hold an arc length about equal to the electrode core diameter at 70–80° travel angle.
Travel steadily to run a straight bead; re-start correctly when the electrode is changed.
Chip slag and brush; inspect the bead width, ripples and spatter.
Run parallel beads, adjusting current and speed to compare results.
practicals.expectedObservations: With correct settings the bead is even in width with fine, regular ripples and little spatter. Too long an arc gives spatter and a wide, flat bead; too fast travel gives a narrow, thin bead.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rule of thumb: current ≈ 40 A per mm of electrode diameter. For 3.2 mm electrodes: 40 × 3.2 = 128 A (practical range about 90–130 A). For 2.5 mm electrodes: 40 × 2.5 = 100 A (range about 70–100 A).
precautions: Keep arc length constant.
Store electrodes dry.
commonMistakes: Electrode sticking from too low current.
Not chipping slag between runs.
examTips: Describe arc length, travel speed, current and electrode angle effects.
Neat, uniform beads earn workmanship marks.

checkQuestions.q: A long arc tends to produce
checkQuestions.explanation: The arc wanders and loses concentration.

checkQuestions.q: Suggested current for a 4 mm electrode is about
The flux coating on an electrode
options: shields the weld and forms slag
checkQuestions.explanation: It produces shielding gas and protective slag.

practicals.title: Preparing a single-V butt joint and welding it
practicals.topic: Preparation of Welding Surfaces and Edges
practicals.aim: To prepare the edges of two plates for a single-V butt weld, tack them and complete the weld in several runs.
safety: Wear goggles and gloves when grinding; keep guards in place.
Full arc-welding PPE when welding.
procedure: Clean the plate edges of rust, mill scale and oil with wire brush, emery and file.
Mark and grind a 30° bevel on each plate (60° included angle), leaving a 1.5 mm root face.
Set the plates with a 2 mm root gap; tack weld at both ends.
Deposit the root run; chip and brush.
Deposit filling and capping runs, cleaning between runs.
Inspect the weld; clean and oil the surface to prevent rust.
practicals.expectedObservations: Full penetration visible on the underside; the cap is slightly convex with even ripples and no undercut.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Bevel width on the face for 10 mm plate with a 1.5 mm root face: (10 − 1.5) × tan 30° = 8.5 × 0.577 = 4.91 mm on each plate. Total gap at the top = 2 × 4.91 + 2 (root gap) ≈ 11.8 mm.
precautions: Keep a uniform root gap.
Clean slag thoroughly between runs.
sourcesOfError: Distortion pulling the plates out of line.
commonMistakes: No root gap, giving lack of penetration.
Skipping post-weld cleaning and oiling.
examTips: Sketch the edge preparation with angles, root face and gap labelled.
Name edge preparations: square, single-V, double-V, J, U, fillet.

checkQuestions.q: The included angle of a standard single-V preparation is about
checkQuestions.explanation: Two 30° bevels.

checkQuestions.q: The purpose of the root gap is to
checkQuestions.explanation: Weld metal must reach the underside.

checkQuestions.q: Double-V preparation is used for
checkQuestions.explanation: It reduces weld metal volume and distortion on thick plate.

practicals.title: Fillet welding a T-joint and a lap joint
practicals.aim: To weld fillet welds on T and lap joints and check leg length and throat thickness.
safety: Full arc welding PPE; screens; ventilation.
procedure: Clean and square the plates.
Set up the T-joint at 90° and tack at both ends.
Weld with the electrode at about 45° between the plates and 70–80° in the direction of travel.
Chip and inspect; repeat on the opposite side.
Set up a lap joint with the overlap at least 3–5 times the plate thickness.
Weld and inspect; measure leg length and throat with the gauge.
practicals.expectedObservations: Equal leg lengths, slightly mitred profile, good fusion into both plates, no undercut.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For an equal-leg fillet weld with 6 mm legs, throat thickness = 0.707 × 6 = 4.24 mm. Lap overlap for 6 mm plate: at least 3 × 6 = 18 mm (5 × 6 = 30 mm preferred).
precautions: Keep the electrode angle at 45° to give equal legs.
Control heat to avoid distortion.
sourcesOfError: Unequal leg lengths from wrong angle.
commonMistakes: Too large a weld causing distortion and waste.
Undercut on the vertical plate.
examTips: Name joints: butt, lap, tee, corner, edge; sketch each.
Show throat calculation.

checkQuestions.q: The throat of an 8 mm equal-leg fillet is about
Electrode angle between the plates for a T-joint is about
checkQuestions.explanation: It bisects the 90° corner.

checkQuestions.q: A groove melted into the base metal beside the weld is
checkQuestions.explanation: Usually caused by excessive current or wrong angle.

practicals.title: Gas welding by the leftward and rightward methods
practicals.aim: To make butt welds in mild steel sheet by the leftward and rightward techniques and compare them.
materials: Mild steel sheet 1.6–3 mm and 5 mm
Copper-coated mild steel filler rod (1.6–3.2 mm)
safety: Follow lighting and shut-down sequences.
Keep hoses away from the flame and hot work.
procedure: Set a neutral flame for the nozzle size.
Tack the sheets with a small gap.
Leftward: start at the right, move the blowpipe to the left with the rod ahead of the flame; blowpipe 60–70°, rod 30–40°.
Rightward: start at the left, move to the right with the rod following the flame; blowpipe 40–50°.
Maintain a molten pool; feed rod into the pool, not the flame.
Inspect bead and penetration and compare.
practicals.expectedObservations: Leftward gives a neat bead on thin sheet; rightward gives better penetration on thicker plate with less filler and faster travel.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Typical guide: leftward for steel up to about 5 mm; rightward for steel over 5 mm. A 3 mm sheet uses a nozzle of about size 3 (consuming roughly 85 L/h of each gas); in 30 minutes this uses about 42 L of acetylene.
precautions: Keep the inner cone 2–3 mm from the pool.
Use a neutral flame.
sourcesOfError: Flame not neutral causing oxidised or hard welds.
commonMistakes: Melting the rod in the flame and dripping it on.
Using leftward on thick plate.
examTips: Compare the two methods in a table: thickness, angles, speed, filler use.
Sketch blowpipe and rod angles.

checkQuestions.q: The rightward method is preferred for
checkQuestions.explanation: It gives better penetration on thick sections.

checkQuestions.q: In leftward welding, the filler rod is
checkQuestions.explanation: The rod leads the blowpipe.

checkQuestions.q: Filler rod should be melted
options: in the flame above the pool
checkQuestions.explanation: This gives fusion with the parent metal.

practicals.title: Marking out, cutting and folding a sheet metal tray
practicals.aim: To develop, mark out, cut and fold a rectangular open tray with corner joints from sheet metal.
materials: Galvanised or black mild steel sheet (e.g. 0.6 mm, 24 SWG)
safety: Wear gloves; sheet edges are razor-sharp.
Remove burrs immediately after cutting.
procedure: Draw the development (net) of the tray with corner tabs.
Mark out on the sheet from a datum edge.
Cut the outline and corner notches with snips.
File edges free of burrs.
Fold the sides to 90° on the folding machine in the correct sequence.
Fold tabs and join the corners by soldering or riveting.
Check dimensions and squareness.
practicals.expectedObservations: A square tray with straight folds and tight corners, matching the drawing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tray 200 × 150 mm base, 30 mm deep: blank size = (200 + 2 × 30) × (150 + 2 × 30) = 260 × 210 mm, plus 10 mm corner tabs. If a wired edge is required on 3 mm wire, add 2.5 × 3 = 7.5 mm to each side: 275 × 225 mm.
precautions: Plan the fold sequence so later folds are possible.
Mark fold lines on the outside face.
sourcesOfError: Material thickness not allowed for in bend lines.
commonMistakes: Cutting off tabs needed for joints.
Folding in the wrong order.
examTips: A neat development drawing with fold lines dotted earns marks.
State the sheet gauge used.

checkQuestions.q: A flat pattern of a 3D object is called a
checkQuestions.explanation: It shows the shape before folding.

checkQuestions.q: Sheet edges are made safe by
options: filing off burrs or wiring/folding the edge
checkQuestions.explanation: This removes sharp edges.

checkQuestions.q: A higher SWG number means the sheet is
checkQuestions.explanation: Gauge numbers increase as thickness decreases.

practicals.title: Making a wired edge on sheet metal
practicals.aim: To strengthen and make safe the edge of a sheet metal article by forming a wired edge.
materials: Mild steel or galvanised wire (e.g. 3 mm)
safety: Wear gloves; keep fingers clear of the folding machine.
procedure: Calculate and mark the wiring allowance along the edge.
Fold the allowance through about 90° then further over a hatchet stake.
Lay the wire in the fold and close the metal around it with a mallet.
Tuck the edge tightly using the wiring machine or the peen of the mallet.
Cut wire ends flush and file smooth.
practicals.expectedObservations: A smooth, round edge fully enclosing the wire, stiffening the article.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Wiring allowance ≈ 2.5 × wire diameter. For 3 mm wire: 2.5 × 3 = 7.5 mm. For 4 mm wire: 10 mm.
precautions: Keep the allowance uniform along the edge.
Close the edge gradually to avoid kinking.
commonMistakes: Too small an allowance — wire not covered.
Hammering marks on the visible face.
examTips: Explain why edges are wired: strength, safety, appearance.
Show allowance calculation.

checkQuestions.q: The wiring allowance for 2 mm wire is about
A wired edge is mainly used to
options: strengthen and make the edge safe
checkQuestions.explanation: It stiffens and removes the sharp edge.

checkQuestions.q: A safe edge made by folding back the metal is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Single or double hems are used where wire is not needed.

practicals.title: Producing a riveted lap joint
practicals.topic: Rivets, Bolts and Nuts, and Screws
practicals.aim: To mark out, drill and close snap-head (or pop) rivets in a lap joint.
materials: Two mild steel strips 1.5 mm thick
safety: Clamp the work for drilling; never hold by hand.
Wear goggles when drilling and riveting.
procedure: Mark the overlap and rivet centres (pitch and edge distance).
Centre punch and drill one plate; clamp both plates and drill through.
De-burr holes.
Insert the rivet; support the head on the dolly.
Draw the plates together with the rivet set.
Upset the tail with the hammer and form the head with the snap.
Repeat; check the joint is tight and heads are central.
practicals.expectedObservations: Rivets are tight, with full, centred heads; plates are drawn together with no gap.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rivet length = grip + 1.5d for a snap head. Grip = 2 × 1.5 = 3 mm; d = 4 mm → length = 3 + 1.5 × 4 = 9 mm. Pitch ≈ 3d = 12 mm; edge distance ≈ 2d = 8 mm.
precautions: Drill holes slightly larger than the rivet (e.g. 4.1 mm).
Draw plates together before heading.
commonMistakes: Rivets too long (bent heads) or too short (incomplete heads).
Edge distance too small, tearing out.
examTips: Name rivet types: snap, pan, countersunk, flat, pop; give uses.
Classify fasteners as permanent (rivets, welds) or temporary (bolts, screws).

checkQuestions.q: Rivet length for a 6 mm grip and 5 mm rivet (snap head) is
Pop rivets are useful when
options: only one side of the work is accessible
checkQuestions.explanation: They are set from one side.

checkQuestions.q: Riveting is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Rivets must be cut or drilled out to remove.

practicals.title: Cutting threads to make a bolt and nut
practicals.topic: Rivets, Bolts and Nuts, and Screws
practicals.aim: To cut an external thread with a die and an internal thread with taps to produce a matching bolt and nut.
apparatus: Tap wrench and M10 taps (taper, second, plug)
materials: Mild steel hexagon or square blank
safety: Clamp the work; wear goggles when drilling.
Remove swarf with a brush, not fingers.
procedure: Chamfer the end of the bar to help the die start.
Hold the bar vertically in the vice; start the die square, turning forward half a turn and back a quarter to break chips.
Use cutting oil; cut the thread to the required length.
Drill the tapping hole in the nut blank (8.5 mm for M10 × 1.5).
Tap the hole using the taper tap, then second and plug taps, keeping the tap square.
Clean and test the bolt and nut together.
practicals.expectedObservations: The nut runs smoothly on the bolt without wobble or binding.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tapping drill size ≈ major diameter − pitch. For M10 × 1.5: 10 − 1.5 = 8.5 mm. For M8 × 1.25: 8 − 1.25 = 6.75 mm (use 6.8 mm).
precautions: Keep tap and die square to the work.
Back off regularly to break chips.
commonMistakes: Wrong tapping drill size (stripped or broken tap).
Forcing the tap, breaking it in the hole.
examTips: Name parts of a thread: major/minor diameter, pitch, crest, root, flank.
Show the tapping drill calculation.

checkQuestions.q: The tapping drill for M12 × 1.75 is about
The first tap used is the
checkQuestions.explanation: Its long lead helps it start straight.

checkQuestions.q: External threads are cut with a
checkQuestions.explanation: Taps cut internal threads.

practicals.title: Soft soldering sheet metal
practicals.aim: To make a soldered lap seam on tinplate or galvanised sheet using a soldering iron and flux.
apparatus: Copper bit soldering iron (or electric iron)
materials: Flux (zinc chloride "killed spirits" or paste flux)
safety: Zinc chloride flux is corrosive: wear gloves and goggles; wash off after soldering.
Ventilate to remove fumes.
procedure: Clean the joint area with emery cloth to bright metal.
File and tin the copper bit.
Apply flux to the joint.
Heat the bit to working temperature (solder flows freely on it).
Tack the seam, then draw the bit slowly along so solder flows into the joint by capillary action.
Wash off flux residue and inspect.
practicals.expectedObservations: Solder runs smoothly into the seam forming a thin, continuous line.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A 60/40 tin–lead solder melts at about 183–190 °C — far below the melting point of steel (about 1 400–1 500 °C) — so soft soldering does not melt the parent metal.
precautions: Keep the bit at the correct temperature.
Clean thoroughly; solder will not wet dirty metal.
sourcesOfError: Bit too cold causing lumpy joints.
commonMistakes: Using corrosive flux on electronics.
Leaving flux residue causing corrosion.
examTips: Distinguish soldering, brazing and welding by temperature and whether parent metal melts.
Name active and passive fluxes.

checkQuestions.q: In soldering, the parent metal
checkQuestions.explanation: Only the solder melts.

checkQuestions.q: Zinc chloride flux is
checkQuestions.explanation: It cleans actively but must be washed off.

checkQuestions.q: Solder fills a lap joint by
checkQuestions.explanation: Molten solder is drawn into narrow gaps.

practicals.title: Forging an eye on a mild steel bar
practicals.aim: To forge an eye on the end of a round bar by bending over the beak of the anvil.
safety: Wear apron, gloves, goggles and boots.
Hold work firmly in correct tongs; keep the floor clear.
Quench or label hot pieces.
procedure: Calculate the length of bar needed for the eye; mark it with a centre punch.
Heat the end to bright red.
Bend the marked length to 90° over the anvil edge.
Reheat and form the eye progressively over the beak (bick), working from the end.
Close the eye and centre it on the bar axis.
Check the inside diameter with a mandrel or gauge; true up and allow to cool.
practicals.expectedObservations: A round, closed eye of uniform section, centred on the bar.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Length for an eye = π × mean diameter. Inside diameter 20 mm, bar diameter 10 mm → mean diameter = 20 + 10 = 30 mm. Length = π × 30 = 94.2 mm.
precautions: Work only at the correct heat; do not hammer below red heat.
Do not overheat (burning).
sourcesOfError: Stretching of the bar during bending.
commonMistakes: Using the inside diameter instead of the mean diameter.
Hammering cold metal, causing cracks.
examTips: Name forging operations: drawing down, upsetting, bending, twisting, punching, forming an eye.
Show the length calculation.

practicals.title: Fabricating a funnel using a template
practicals.aim: To develop the pattern of a conical frustum by radial-line development, make a template and fabricate a funnel.
safety: Wear gloves when cutting and forming sheet.
procedure: Draw the elevation of the frustum and extend the sides to find the apex.
Calculate the slant heights and sector angle (or develop graphically).
Draw the development on card with seam allowance and cut it out as a template.
Transfer to sheet and cut.
Roll the cone on the funnel stake.
Lock or solder the seam; add the spout and a wired or hemmed top edge.
practicals.expectedObservations: The cone forms with the seam edges meeting evenly; top and bottom openings are circular.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Funnel cone: top Ø150 mm, bottom Ø30 mm, height 100 mm. Full cone height = 100 × 150/(150 − 30) = 125 mm. Slant height L = √(125² + 75²) = 145.8 mm; small slant l = 145.8 × 30/150 = 29.2 mm. Sector angle = 360 × 75/145.8 = 185.2°.
precautions: Add seam allowance to one edge only.
Check template by rolling before cutting metal.
sourcesOfError: Small angle errors widening the seam gap.
commonMistakes: Using the vertical height instead of slant height as the radius.
Forgetting seam allowance.
examTips: Show the development method clearly; examiners award marks for construction.
Name development methods: parallel line, radial line, triangulation.

checkQuestions.explanation: Radial lines from the apex.

checkQuestions.explanation: True length of the sloping side.

checkQuestions.q: A template is used to
checkQuestions.explanation: It saves time and ensures repeatability.

practicals.title: Inspecting welds for defects
practicals.aim: To identify common weld defects by visual inspection and simple tests and state their causes and remedies.
materials: Sample welds with defects: porosity, undercut, overlap, slag inclusion, lack of penetration, cracks, excessive spatter
safety: Wear goggles during bend or break tests.
Etching chemicals are handled only by the teacher.
procedure: Clean each weld of slag and spatter.
Examine the face and root visually with the lens.
Measure bead size and leg length.
Saw a cross-section of some samples to reveal inclusions and penetration.
Perform a nick-break or bend test on a sample.
Record defect, likely cause and remedy.
practicals.expectedObservations: Porosity shows as holes; undercut as a groove at the toe; slag inclusion as dark spots in the section; lack of penetration as an unfused root.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Acceptance example: a specification allows undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm. A measured undercut of 0.8 mm exceeds this by 0.3 mm, so the weld is rejected and repaired.
precautions: Clean welds before inspection.
Use good lighting.
sourcesOfError: Hidden internal defects not visible from the surface.
commonMistakes: Confusing spatter with porosity.
examTips: Table: defect – cause – remedy is the expected format.
Mention destructive and non-destructive tests.

checkQuestions.q: Porosity is mainly caused by
checkQuestions.explanation: Gas is trapped in the weld.

checkQuestions.q: Slag inclusion is prevented by
checkQuestions.explanation: Slag trapped under later runs causes inclusions.

checkQuestions.q: Undercut is often caused by
checkQuestions.explanation: High current melts away the toe.

practicals.title: Interpreting welding symbols on drawings
practicals.aim: To read and draw standard welding symbols showing weld type, size, location and finish.
safety: Not applicable beyond normal classroom safety.
procedure: Identify the parts of a welding symbol: arrow line, reference line, basic symbol, dimensions, supplementary symbols.
Identify basic symbols: fillet, square butt, single-V, double-V, plug, spot.
Interpret whether the weld is on the arrow side or other side.
Read the size and length dimensions.
Draw symbols for given joints.
Sketch the actual welds that the symbols describe.
practicals.expectedObservations: Symbols match the welds required; arrow-side and other-side conventions are correctly applied.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A fillet symbol marked "6 ◺ 4 × 50 (100)" means a 6 mm fillet, 4 welds each 50 mm long at 100 mm pitch: total weld length = 4 × 50 = 200 mm.
precautions: Follow the standard (ISO 2553 or AWS A2.4) used on the drawing.
commonMistakes: Confusing arrow side and other side.
examTips: Sketch the basic symbols accurately.
State the meaning of the field-weld flag and weld-all-round circle.
